hook: Read a quiet German short story the way it wants to be read: through gestures, objects and what nobody says aloud.
intro: A literary Kurzgeschichte of about 430 words, „Die blaue Tasse“. It starts abruptly in an everyday moment – „Das Wasser kochte schon, als das Telefon klingelte.“ – and follows one Tuesday morning of Brenner, a widower whose wife Ruth has died some months before („seit der Beerdigung“). His daughter Katrin rings, as every Tuesday, to push him to view a two-room flat. Nothing is explained: Brenner's grief shows only in gestures – he takes out the blue cup „aus der Ruth immer getrunken hatte“, leaves it empty at her place by the window, washes it although it is not dirty. The story is told in the third person, close to Brenner, in understatement („Zwei Zimmer, dachte er, das reicht für einen.“), and it ends open, with one telling last sentence. The eight questions ask about the plot, the narrative perspective, the symbol, what the dialogue leaves unsaid, and how to read the ending.
tips[0].title: Kurzgeschichte conventions – find them in this text
tips[0].text: Abrupt start without introduction, an ordinary moment, few characters, no explanation of feelings, understatement, a symbolic object (Dingsymbol) and an open ending. When a question asks what a gesture "means", the answer is an interpretation the text supports – not a fact it states, and not a decision it never shows.
tips[0].trap: Options with „endgültig“ or „auf jeden Fall“ usually claim more than an open Kurzgeschichte says.
tips[0].check.why: The gesture supports an interpretation, avoidance. 'Definitely never' claims more than the line shows, and the sender is never mentioned.

tips[1].title: Perspective: personal narration in the third person
tips[1].text: The narrator stays inside Brenner's perception („dachte er“, „Er hörte, wie …“) but never names his feelings. Katrin is seen only through what he hears. So the reader has to infer grief, resistance and hesitation from what Brenner does and does not do.
tips[1].check.why: dachte sie marks personal narration: we hear her thoughts from close up, without the narrator commenting.
tips[2].title: The symbol: follow the object through the text
tips[2].text: Track the blue cup: taken out, not put back, carried empty to Ruth's place, washed though clean, not returned to its shelf, put on the windowsill. Each step is a small decision about how much of Ruth stays in his day. The white cup with the crack is its quiet counterpart – the one that is actually used.
tips[2].check.why: An object that keeps coming back carries feeling the text doesn't name: leaving the coat where it was keeps her present.
tips[3].title: The last sentence links back
tips[3].text: A telling last sentence often picks up an earlier detail. Here „Von dort … sieht man den Hof“ echoes why Ruth sat by the window – „weil sie sehen wollte, wer auf den Hof kam“. Read the ending against that earlier sentence, and resist closing what the text leaves open.
tips[3].check.why: The last sentence echoes the earlier detail, so read it against that: he now sits where she waited. Moving out or forgetting is nowhere in the text.
remember[0]: Kurzgeschichte: abrupt start, everyday moment, understatement, Dingsymbol, open ending.
remember[1]: Personal narration (Er-Form, close to one figure): feelings are shown, never explained.
remember[2]: Follow the symbolic object step by step – each gesture is a small decision.
remember[3]: Read the last sentence against an earlier detail it echoes.
remember[4]: Distrust options that close an open ending („endgültig“, „auf jeden Fall“).
exam: Short stories with open endings are a C2 exam reading text — and the core of German literature from Borchert to today.
